intro: Practice the pointer-replacement pattern used in BST remove() - this is an actual Exam 2 question. Add pruneFullSubtreesSize3() to BinarySearchTree.java so that it removes every full size-3 subtree (a root with exactly two leaf children), then paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back. The same recursive return pattern - returning the updated subtree root - applies directly to EditorTrees Milestone 3 deletion.
hints: A full size-3 subtree has a root with exactly two non-null children and no grandchildren; both children are leaves.
Visit nodes bottom-up (post-order): recursively prune children before deciding whether the current node is the root of a full size-3 subtree.

In the recursive helper, return NULL_NODE when the current node qualifies (left != NULL_NODE, right != NULL_NODE, left.left == NULL_NODE, left.right == NULL_NODE, right.left == NULL_NODE, right.right == NULL_NODE); otherwise return this.

intro: Practice the BST search path pattern - this is an actual Exam 2 question. Add shortestWordAlongPath(String target) to BinarySearchTree.java that walks the BST search path toward the target and returns the shortest String encountered along the way, then paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back. Practices the Tree Navigation pattern from the Exam 2 review.
hints: Follow the standard BST search path from the root toward the target, comparing at each node exactly as contains() does.
Track the shortest String seen so far as you walk the path, updating it whenever you find a String with fewer characters than the current best.
In the recursive helper, pass the current best down and return it; there is no need to backtrack, because you only visit nodes on the single root-to-target path.

intro: Practice full-tree traversal with a depth parameter - this is an actual Exam 2 question. Add countLeftNodesAtDepth(int depth) to BinarySearchTree.java, then paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back. The same recursive accumulator pattern (traverse all nodes, count at a specific depth) applies to EditorTrees Milestone 1 traversal by rank.
hints: Recurse with a depth counter: at each node, reduce the target depth by 1; when the counter hits 0, the current node is at the target depth.
A node is a left child when it was reached by following a parent's left pointer; pass an isLeftChild boolean down the recursion, and count when depth==0 and isLeftChild==true.
Base case: if the current node is NULL_NODE, return 0. The root call should pass isLeftChild=false so the root is never counted even when depth==0.

intro: Add isHeightBalanced() to BinarySearchTree.java - the height-balance property that EditorTrees M2 enforces automatically via balance codes. HW5 asks you to check this property as an explicit method; EditorTrees requires maintaining it after every insertion and deletion. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: A tree is height-balanced if every node satisfies |height(left subtree) - height(right subtree)| <= 1.
Recurse through all nodes: for each BinaryNode, check both children recursively AND check the balance condition at the current node.
Use the existing height() helper to compute left and right heights at each node, then return false early if the difference exceeds 1 at any node.

intro: Add getSumOfHeights() to BinarySearchTree.java that computes the sum of heights of all nodes using the height() method you already have. HW5 and EditorTrees M2 both rely on height computation at every node; this drill builds intuition for how heights change as the tree grows. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: The height of a single leaf node is 0, and the height of NULL_NODE is -1, so a root-only tree has sum 0.
Recurse through all nodes and accumulate height(node) for each non-null node; your existing height() method returns the correct value at each node.
When you add a symmetric sibling (e.g., both left and right children are leaves), their heights are both 0 and the root's height rises to 1, so the sum stays the same or grows depending on the shape.

intro: Add a BinarySearchTree(int maxDepth) constructor that builds a complete full binary tree with each node's value equal to its depth. HW5 and EditorTrees M1 both require building tree structure by wiring up parent-child pointers recursively - this drill practices that construction pattern. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: A full binary tree of maxDepth 0 is just a root node with value 0; depth 1 adds a left child and right child both with value 1.

Use a recursive helper that takes the current depth and the maxDepth: if currentDepth > maxDepth, return NULL_NODE; otherwise create a node with value currentDepth and set its children by recursing with currentDepth+1.
toStructuredString() format wraps left subtree in brackets, then the node value, then right subtree in brackets; mirror this structure in your mental model to verify depth-1: [[1]0[1]].

intro: Add removeMin() to BinarySearchTree.java that removes and returns the minimum element (the leftmost node). Uses the same one-child pointer-swap pattern as remove(), and the same return-value propagation pattern required for EditorTrees Milestone 3 deletion. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: The minimum is always the leftmost node; keep following left pointers until you find a node whose left child is NULL_NODE.
Once found, unlink the minimum by replacing it with its right child (which may be NULL_NODE), exactly the same pointer-swap as removing a node with zero or one child in remove().
Return the data value from the removed node. In the recursive helper, when node.left == NULL_NODE, set the parent's left pointer to node.right and return node.data.

intro: Add getPreOrderList() to BinarySearchTree.java that collects all elements in pre-order (root first, then left subtree, then right subtree) into an ArrayList<T>. HW6 PreOrderBuildTree requires understanding exactly what pre-order encodes - this drill makes that encoding concrete. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: Pre-order means: add the current node's data FIRST, then recurse left, then recurse right; root always comes before its descendants.
Pass an ArrayList into the recursive helper (or build one from recursive results): add current node data, then append the left subtree's pre-order list, then the right subtree's.
For a balanced 3-node tree with root 10, left 5, right 15: pre-order visits 10 -> 5 -> 15, so list.get(0)==10 and list.get(1)==5.

intro: Add buildSearchPathList(T item) to BinarySearchTree.java returning an ArrayList of all values on the BST search path from root to item, or an empty list if the item is not found. This is a 2020-21 practice Exam 2 question using the same O(height) navigation pattern as shortestWordAlongPath. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: Walk the BST search path exactly as contains() does: left if item < current, right if item > current. Add the current node's value to the result list before recursing.
Propagate failure upward: if the recursive call returns an empty list, the item was not found in that subtree — return empty without prepending the current node.
Base case: if current node is NULL_NODE, return an empty list (item not found). If current.data.equals(item), return a list containing only current.data.

intro: Add countSiblingDiffGreaterThan(int threshold) to BinarySearchTree.java that counts nodes whose two children have a value difference strictly greater than the threshold (right.data - left.data > threshold, both children must exist). This is a 2020-21 practice Exam 2 question using the same full-tree recursive accumulator pattern as getSumOfHeights. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: Traverse every node (full-tree traversal, not BST search) and accumulate a count — same structure as getSumOfHeights() or size().
At each BinaryNode, count 1 if both children are not NULL_NODE AND (right.data - left.data) > threshold; otherwise count 0. Then add the counts from left and right subtrees.
The difference is always right.data - left.data (positive, since BSTs keep right > left), so no absolute value needed. Both children must be non-null — a node with only one child does not qualify.

intro: Add weightedHeight() to BinarySearchTree.java that returns the sum of (height × size) for every node in the tree. This is the computer part of the Spring 2021 practice Exam 3, and earns efficiency points only if it runs in O(N) with a single traversal — no calling height() or size() separately on each node. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: A naive approach calls height() and size() at every node, giving O(N²) — to earn efficiency points, compute both in one pass using a helper that returns a container holding {height, size, weightedHeightContribution}.

Define a helper class or use an int[] of length 3. At each node: height = 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight); size = 1 + leftSize + rightSize; contribution = height*size + leftContribution + rightContribution.
Base case for NULL_NODE: return height=-1, size=0, contribution=0. The root call then returns the total contribution directly.

intro: Add pruneLeaves() to BinarySearchTree.java that removes all leaf nodes from the tree. This is a Winter 2016-17 practice Exam 2 question using the same return-updated-subtree pointer pattern as remove(). Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: A leaf is a node whose both left and right children are NULL_NODE. In the recursive helper, return NULL_NODE when the current node is a leaf.
Use the same return-updated-subtree pattern as remove(): node.left = pruneHelper(node.left); node.right = pruneHelper(node.right); then check if both children are now NULL_NODE.
Process children before deciding whether to prune the current node (post-order): prune the children first, then check if the current node has become a leaf.

intro: Add branchPoint(T x, T y) to BinarySearchTree.java that returns the value at the deepest common ancestor of the BST search paths for x and y, or null if both paths end at the same NULL_NODE. This is a Winter 2016-17 practice Exam 2 question with efficiency points for O(height) — the same structured descent as shortestWordAlongPath. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: At each node, compare x and y to the current node's data: if both go left, recurse left; if both go right, recurse right; if they diverge (or one matches), the current node is the branch point.
This runs in O(height) because you follow a single path from root to the branch point — never backtrack or visit both subtrees.
Edge case: if x.compareTo(current) == 0 OR y.compareTo(current) == 0, the current node is on both search paths (one ends here), so it is the branch point.

intro: Add countOneChildParents() to BinarySearchTree.java that returns the number of nodes that have exactly one child (either left or right, but not both). This is a Winter 2016-17 practice Exam 2 question using the same full-tree recursive accumulator pattern as size(). Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: Traverse all nodes (full-tree, not BST search) and accumulate a count — same structure as size().
A node has exactly one child when: (left == NULL_NODE) XOR (right == NULL_NODE). In Java: (left == NULL_NODE) != (right == NULL_NODE).
Return 0 for NULL_NODE as the base case; otherwise return (isOneChildParent ? 1 : 0) + countHelper(left) + countHelper(right).

intro: Practice combining height computation with a structural predicate - this appears on the Final Exam. Add countOddOnlyIf() to BinarySearchTree.java that counts nodes whose Integer value is odd and whose left subtree height is strictly less than their right subtree height. The same height-comparison logic underpins EditorTrees M2 balance code maintenance. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: A node counts only if two conditions are both true: its value is odd (value % 2 != 0), and height(left child) < height(right child).
Recurse through all nodes and sum the count: at each node, check both conditions independently, then add the counts from left and right subtrees.
When you insert 101 as the right child of 81 (odd), height(left of 81) becomes -1 and height(right of 81) becomes 0, so 81 satisfies both conditions and contributes 1 to the count.
